message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise overview of the most important tenant rights under Texas law. These rights apply to most residential leases (apartments, houses, condos, etc.) and are enforced by the Texas Property Code, local ordinances, and the Texas Attorney General’s Office. | Category | Key Rights | Practical Tips | |----------|------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Inspect the unit with the landlord before moving out and document any damage. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity).
• Repairs must be made within a reasonable time after notice. | • Report problems in writing (email or text) and keep copies.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent or pay for repairs and deduct from rent (see “Rent‑Withholding” below). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease specifies them and they are **reasonable** (not punitive). | • Keep records of all payments.
• If you’re late, communicate with the landlord promptly. | | **Rent‑Withholding** | • If the landlord fails to maintain habitability, you may **withhold rent** until repairs are made.
• You must give written notice and allow a **reasonable period** (usually 30 days) for repairs. | • Document all communication.
• If the landlord refuses to repair, you can file a claim in small‑claims court. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of all entries. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord cannot enter without notice, except in emergencies. | • If you suspect unauthorized entry, document it and consider filing a complaint. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes (under the Fair Housing Act). | • Report discrimination to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Attorney General. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a lease with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month).
• Landlord must provide a **written notice** of termination. | • Keep copies of all notices. | | **Security Deposit Deductions** | • Landlord may deduct for:
- Unpaid rent
- Damage beyond normal wear & tear
- Cleaning costs if the unit is not left in a clean condition
- Replacement of lost keys or locks | • Landlord must provide an itemized list of deductions. | | **Right to Repair** | • If the landlord fails to repair, you may:
- Pay for repairs and deduct from rent
- File a claim in small‑claims court
- Seek a court order for repair | • Keep receipts and documentation. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the Texas **eviction procedure**: written notice, filing a lawsuit, court hearing, and sheriff’s eviction if ordered.
• Common grounds: non‑payment of rent, lease violations, or owner’s intent to occupy. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Seek legal counsel if you receive an eviction notice. | | **Tenant’s Right to a Written Lease** | • While not required, a written lease protects both parties. | • Always sign a lease and keep a copy. | | **Local Ordinances** | • Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas, Houston) have additional tenant protections (rent control, eviction moratoria, etc.). | • Check your city’s housing department for local rules. | --- #### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read the Lease** – Understand rent amount, due date, security deposit limits, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts. 3. **Know Your Local Ordinances** – Some cities add extra protections. 4. **Communicate in Writing** – Email or text is preferable; keep copies. 5. **Seek Legal Help Early** – If you face eviction or major disputes, consult a tenant‑rights attorney or a local legal aid organization. --- #### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Housing** | Tenant‑rights guides, complaint forms, and legal assistance. | | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Information on fair housing, landlord‑tenant laws, and local programs. | | **Local Legal Aid Societies** | Free or low‑cost legal advice for tenants. | | **HUD (U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development)** | Fair housing complaints and resources. | | **Texas Tenants’ Association** | Advocacy, education, and support groups. | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, a reasonable notice for entry, protection against discrimination, and the ability to withhold rent or seek legal remedies if the landlord fails to meet obligations. Always keep records, communicate clearly, and know where to turn for help if disputes arise.
